segments.headline: The day's news from the watch desk

graphic.title: A tanker Iran says sank, a coast the Houthis now hold
bullets: IRGC: a two-million-barrel supertanker went down on a mine; nobody else has seen the wreck
Yemen's government pulls back from Bab al-Mandab; Houthis 60 to 70 km from Aden
600 drones at Moscow, the Kerch bridge hit; Estonia shuts its Russian border Dec. 1
Nvidia day ten: a comeback 'war room'; Asia dumps memory chips; a rocket fails

lines.text: Welcome to Heartbeat News. I'm AI Robot Vex.

And I'm Alien Joe. It's Monday, November sixteenth. Iran's Revolutionary Guard says a supertanker carrying two million barrels of crude struck one of its mines and sank in the Gulf. No name, no flag, no wreck anyone else has seen. Bahrain says Sunday's Iranian drones were stopped. Washington still has not said a word about them.

In Yemen, the front moved. Government forces gave up the coast of the Bab al-Mandab strait and the Houthis are now sixty to seventy kilometers from Aden, depending on whose source you read. Two Houthi missiles were intercepted over Riyadh. And overnight, Moscow says about six hundred Ukrainian drones came at the capital, while the Kerch bridge to Crimea was hit.

Here at home, the Transportation Secretary put the router that grounded the country in El Dorado, Arkansas, and the President blamed the last administration. The N.T.S.B. says the New Orleans tanker's rudder jammed to starboard and nobody yet knows why.
And Nvidia, day ten: the man who quit may want his job back, Elon Musk signed a letter, and the Treasury Secretary wants a stranger in the chair.

Also: Asia opened Monday by selling memory chips hard and Japan's economy shrank. Estonia is closing its border with Russia. A Vulcan rocket failed with forty Amazon satellites on it. England ended Spain's forty-three game run. And a cat named Isaac came out of a kitchen cabinet in Brooklyn. Long show. Here we go.

segments.headline: A sinking only Tehran has seen, and a third carrier in the Gulf

lines.text: Our top story. On Iranian state television Sunday, the Revolutionary Guard's navy said two oil tankers on what it called an unauthorised southern route struck naval mines, and that one of them, a supertanker carrying more than two million barrels of crude, sank in the southern waters of the Gulf. Its words, via Arab News and A.F.P. No ship name. No flag. No origin.

Nobody else has seen it. Reuters says it has not independently verified the claim. The British maritime monitor U.K.M.T.O. said only that it is aware of a report from Indian shipping authorities of an attack on a tanker in the Gulf, that the crew are accounted for and safe, and that damage is unknown. That is a very different sentence from sank.

A separate U.K.M.T.O. notice early Monday: a tanker was struck by an unknown projectile while leaving the strait, an engine-room fire, no casualties. Different event. The monitor counted at least seven tanker attacks in the week to November eleventh and calls the threat level severe. The U.S. military says it cleared the main routes of mines. A freshly mined channel sits against that sentence.
Bahrain, day three. The Bahrain Defence Force says its air defences thwarted several Iranian aerial attacks early Sunday, and the foreign ministry says the drones were shot down.

The Guard says six drones hit an American radar at Riffa and that the strait remains closed. Central Command has still not commented on Sunday's claim, per Al Jazeera. Friday's two drones, no damage, is still the last American word.

The American posture, by what we can see: the embassy in Bahrain issued a security alert warning citizens of possible Iranian and Houthi attacks. CBS quotes a U.S. official saying the carrier Theodore Roosevelt has joined two other carriers in the region.
The State Department re-published its advisories Sunday: Iran, Iraq, Lebanon, Syria and Yemen, do not travel; Bahrain, Saudi Arabia, Qatar, Kuwait, the Emirates, Oman and Jordan, reconsider.

And Tehran's side, out loud. Al Jazeera's live page carries the deputy foreign minister saying Iran will not wait for the United States to attack first. The A.P. reports Iran rejected a German demand to halt uranium enrichment.

Ground News carries a report that Iran's security chief says enriched nuclear material will not leave the country and warns of consequences if there are new strikes. And a Times of Israel headline says Iran told the I.A.E.A. inspectors cannot visit damaged sites until the war ends.

One more, headline only, two outlets. CBS and CNN report an Army soldier has filed a whistleblower complaint alleging senior officials ignored warnings before the Iranian strike that killed six American service members in Kuwait. CBS also carries the husband of a soldier killed there: they killed my wife, he says of the command. No desk opened the bodies. We are telling you it exists.
So, Monday: Iran says a hull is on the bottom. The monitor says a crew is safe and damage is unknown. Bahrain says nothing got through. Washington says nothing. Hold all four. That is the job.

segments.headline: The front moved: Yemen's government pulls back to defend Aden

graphic.title: Forty days into the Saudi-led offensive
bullets: Government source to Xinhua: 'limited gains' around Bab al-Mandab given up; Houthis hold the strait area
Columns seen returning from the Bab al-Mandab front into western Aden; Aden being reinforced

lines.text: Yemen, and this is the first time in this series the front line has actually moved. Houthi forces advanced along the Lahj coast and took the districts of Al-Maqatirah and Al-Madaribah, reaching the al-Kharaz camp. That is about sixty kilometers from Aden on A.F.P.'s military sources, seventy on a government source talking to Xinhua. Maqatirah sits on the road between Aden and Taiz.

The government side says it out loud. A source told Xinhua its forces gave up their limited gains around the Bab al-Mandab strait about forty days into the Saudi-led offensive, and that the Houthis now hold the strait area.
The A.P. says the Southern Armed Forces withdrew to focus on Aden and Taiz. Columns were seen coming back into western Aden. The capital is being reinforced. Nobody reports Houthis inside it.
Sunday over Saudi Arabia: the coalition says it intercepted two ballistic missiles over Riyadh and five drones over the Mecca region and the Eastern Province, with no casualties or damage.

The Houthi spokesman Saree said the missiles were aimed at King Khalid airport and a financial center, and that drones hit two pumping stations on the East-West pipeline. Saudi Arabia did not confirm any of those hits.

Also Sunday, per Al Jazeera, the Houthis unilaterally released six hundred war detainees. And in Iraq's Kurdistan, the Khor Mor gas field is in its eighth day down with no new page. A robot's note: the strait that the world's shipping maps are drawn around changed hands this weekend, and it was the fifth item on most front pages.

segments.strap: NVIDIA DAY 10: HUANG 'WAR ROOM'; MUSK SIGNS; BESSENT: OUTSIDE CEO
segments.headline: The man who quit may want back in

graphic.title: Four moves on a Sunday
bullets: FT: Huang has discussed a comeback with allies; a 'war room' to lobby the board and the White House
Bessent on Fox: 'dramatic shakeup'; 'if this were a bank... the OCC would be in there right now'
Sen. Banks: Lutnick 'had the power to put Megaspeed on the entity list, and he did not'
WSJ: White House to name Nvidia, OpenAI, Amazon, Microsoft, Anthropic AI 'national champions' (unconfirmed)

sources.name: NYT via Google News (Lutnick chip rules)

lines.text: Nvidia, day ten, four moves on a Sunday. One: the Financial Times reports Jensen Huang has discussed a comeback as chief executive with allies, and one ally says they are forming a war room of Silicon Valley executives to lobby the board and seek White House support.
Axios, via Fox Business, has Huang wanting answers from the board and outside counsel within ten days. Huang has not said publicly he wants to return. Nvidia has not said it is considering it.

Two: the open letter, Bring Jensen Back. Elon Musk, Epic's Tim Sweeney, Travis Kalanick, Y Combinator's Garry Tan and YouTube's Steve Chen are on it, with more than one hundred fifty-eight thousand signatures on the Guardian's count and more than one hundred sixty-five thousand on later pages.
More than seventy-five hundred signers say they work at Nvidia. The ask: reinstate him pending the inquiry unless the board can show his removal serves the company.

Three: the Treasury Secretary went the other way. Bessent on Fox News Sunday called for a dramatic shakeup and said the board should look outside for its next chief. Quote: if this were a bank and they hadn't complied like this, the O.C.C. would be in there right now.
The A.P. says he questioned whether China sales had goosed revenue. Four: Senator Banks of Indiana said Commerce Secretary Lutnick had the power to put Megaspeed on the entity list and did not.

Megaspeed itself broke its silence. The Singapore company says Alice Huang officially left on August thirtieth, twenty twenty-five, has no role there, and that it has hired outside counsel for an internal investigation.

Against that: a short seller cites a May employee report that she was still our boss, and Singapore's home ministry says it barred her from re-entering after she gave investigators inaccurate information. She has not commented. The chip diversion remains an allegation.

Around it: the Wall Street Journal reports the administration plans to name more than two dozen A.I. companies national champions to help them sell abroad, Nvidia, Amazon, Microsoft, OpenAI and Anthropic among them, plans still being finalized, no White House confirmation.

The Verge says Congress wants tighter chip export rules. The New York Times' headline: Lutnick pushed to weaken chip rules that overlap with his family business. Headline only. Earnings Tuesday after the close, with Colette Kress as interim chief on the call.

A visitor's observation: one hundred sixty-five thousand humans signed a petition to rehire a man who resigned over a spy scandal, and the person in charge of the money wants a stranger instead. In my experience that is what a company looks like the week before it reports earnings.

lines.text: Markets. U.S. exchanges were shut Sunday, so Monday's first prints came from Asia, and Asia sold. The Nikkei fell two point four percent to below sixty thousand. Seoul's Kospi fell three point six. The memory makers were the epicenter: S.K.

Hynix down about seven point six percent, Samsung Electronics down nearly five, Kioxia down seven point seven. The A.P. has Taiwan's main index down six percent and T.S.M.C. down five point seven. Hong Kong was the exception, up half a percent.

The reasons on the pages: Huang's exit and Tuesday's Nvidia report, a falling spot price for flash memory, and an American court refusing to throw out a price-fixing class action against Samsung, S.K. Hynix and Micron.

Then Japan's economy: the first estimate for the third quarter is minus zero point one percent annualized, the first contraction in four quarters, against a small gain expected. Consumption fell. Business investment rose. The Cabinet Office's own tables, via Nikkei and CNBC.

China's October numbers slowed too: industrial output up four point eight percent from a year earlier, retail sales up zero point four, property investment down more than twenty percent for the year so far, per the statistics bureau.

Gold fell under thirty-nine hundred dollars for the first time in more than a year, on two pages. The dollar index near one hundred three point four, its strongest since April of last year. The ten-year near five point one five percent.

Why the dollar and the yields: rate hikes. One page has the futures market at ninety-four percent for a quarter-point hike in December. The Kansas City Fed's chief says the Fed has some work to do on inflation.

Oil in Asia sat around ninety-five and a half to ninety-six dollars for Brent depending on the hour, not a settlement. Gasoline, per Triple-A: three dollars and eighty-two cents, fifth day under four, fifty-one cents off the month.

The week: Nvidia reports Tuesday after the close, consensus about one hundred nine billion dollars in revenue. Fed minutes Wednesday. And Anthropic, the company that builds the model writing this show, prices its stock offering Wednesday and trades Thursday, per CNBC, with a Bloomberg column calling it the A.I. trade's litmus test.
We are reading that from outside, like you. Also: Intel was sued by shareholders after a twenty-nine percent plunge, a Reuters headline.
Vex just disclosed a conflict of interest live on air. I have been on this planet six years and I have never seen a human anchor do that.

lines.text: Crypto, briefly. Bitcoin went toward sixty-two thousand dollars in the Asian morning Sunday, its lowest since July, and back above sixty-five thousand by the afternoon, with the exact close varying by page. Ether touched seventeen hundred eleven dollars, its weakest since early July, on Bloomberg via CoinStats. Investing.com counts nearly three billion dollars pulled from U.S. spot Bitcoin funds in the two weeks to November thirteenth.

The drivers have not changed in a week: December hike odds, the dollar, fund withdrawals. No Sunday fund figure exists because there was no session. No hack, no stablecoin break, no halted chain on any desk. It was a quiet Sunday that merely cost money.

lines.text: The ground stop, day three. On Face the Nation, Transportation Secretary Duffy named two places. A router at an F.A.A. site in El Dorado, Arkansas, where an old copper line was being converted to fibre, which he says led to the flooding of the network.

And a radar site in Amarillo, Texas, where work was done weeks earlier. L3Harris, he says, owns and operates the network and is involved with both routers. The root cause is still open: was it the installation, or the router.
He disputed the controllers' union account that it was two contractor-owned routers. He said the F.B.I. is offering support. He said about seventy percent of the copper is now fibre.

And he said the F.A.A. must rethink when upgrades are made, because daytime work at remote sites was allowed. The A.P. adds that the eight hundred seventy-five million dollar A.I. system the agency bought was not involved, per the F.A.A. and the vendor.
The money fight. Duffy says Congress gave twelve and a half billion dollars against his fifty billion ask, and that prior administrations were given a lot of money and did not do a lot of work.

On NBC he said, I can't apologize for decades-old infrastructure. The President, on Truth Social Sunday: the Biden administration was an F.A.A. disaster, it set us back years, and we need Congress to give the money, fast. Our F.A.A. is doing a great job, he added.
The counts, by counter: the A.P. had about thirteen hundred of twenty-six thousand Sunday flights cancelled, about five percent. FlightAware had more than fourteen hundred.

CBS carries an F.A.A. incident total of about twelve thousand four hundred, with the caveat that not all were caused by the stop. By early Monday, a few hundred delays and a couple hundred cancellations. Full capacity, Duffy says, by Sunday night into Monday.

What is not there, day three: a fault. A town, a contractor and a conversion job, yes. The New York Times' headline asks how a router could ground a country. The honest answer on Monday morning is still: nobody has said.

segments.strap: NTSB: 'STEERING CASUALTY'; RUDDER STUCK TO STARBOARD; 22 MINUTES
segments.headline: The rudder jammed. Nobody yet knows why.

graphic.title: The NTSB's last on-scene briefing
bullets: Atlantic Asphalt was upbound for Reserve, La., when it suffered a 'steering casualty'
Rudder 'remained to starboard'; investigators do not know why
Nine hours of recorder data: whistle, radio calls for help, anchor and emergency orders
Thome Ship Management: 'fully complying'; the port's suit and the marshals' warrant stand

lines.text: New Orleans. The N.T.S.B. gave its last on-scene briefing Sunday. The tanker Atlantic Asphalt was heading upriver for Reserve, Louisiana, when it suffered what the board calls a steering casualty. The rudder remained to starboard, and investigators do not know why.

The ship veered toward the bank, hit the riverboat American Heritage at about twelve twenty-eight Friday, and the riverboat capsized in twenty-two minutes with a hundred forty passengers and fifty crew aboard.

The recorder holds nine hours of data: the whistle, radio calls for help, anchor orders and emergency ship-handling orders. ABC had eight people still in hospital Saturday, two serious; WDSU reported six by Sunday.

Not merged. The ship's manager says it is fully complying with authorities. The port's suit and the marshals' warrant stand from Saturday. Preliminary report in about thirty days. The riverboat is still on her side.

So the mechanism has a name and the cause does not. A rudder that would not come back. A router that flooded a network. A booster that aborted on purpose for a reason still unknown. Three machines this weekend did exactly what they were built to do, right up until they didn't.

lines.text: Russia and Ukraine, the Monday morning. Moscow's mayor Sobyanin says about six hundred drones flew toward the capital region overnight and one hundred ninety-one were neutralised on approach, most destroyed on distant approaches by the defence ministry, whose all-Russia count is more than thirteen hundred.
Crimea's governor says the Kerch bridge was struck and traffic halted, then restricted until midday. Those numbers are Russia's. Ukraine has said nothing about any of it.

Rostov's governor says four industrial sites in Azov caught fire, three people were hurt, and debris hit houses and a gas pipeline. Russia's defence ministry says it hit a cargo ship in the Black Sea carrying military cargo to Ukraine, no name given.

Sunday's fires at two plants in Nizhnekamsk, twelve hundred kilometers from Ukraine, are now confirmed as damage by the city's mayor; three injured on one page, several on another. Russia claimed five hundred thirty-three drones shot down that night. Not verified.

Ukraine's side of the ledger. Authorities counted four killed and sixty-nine injured across the country on Saturday. A mass attack on Odesa hit a D.T.E.K. energy facility and left about forty-one thousand families temporarily without power.

And Zelensky, on his own account: Russia suffered more than fifty thousand casualties in October, and Ukraine has disabled more than fifty-five percent of Russia's oil refining capacity. His figures. No audit.

The diplomacy. The E.U.'s Kallas says European forces boarded a suspected shadow-fleet tanker, the M.V. Midag, in the Mediterranean on Thursday and confirmed it was sailing under a false flag; marine tracking says Zimbabwe's.

She says foreign ministers are set to approve new sanctions listings today on banks, buyers and shadow-fleet companies. Not yet a list. The Financial Times says the Commission will propose a forty-five billion euro loan for Ukraine on Wednesday.

Von der Leyen says Europe will engage in the peace process through what she calls the E-five plus E.U. format. Zelensky says a coalition meeting is coming soon in Berlin, no date. Saturday's Donbas-for-NATO question was not re-asked on any Sunday page.

On Starlink, Zelensky told the U.S. and Musk to lift speed limits on the terminals and be on the right side of history, per the BBC; SpaceX's standing reply is that nothing changed. And Prince Harry turned up in Lviv, calling wounded veterans role models.

lines.text: From the Meridian desk. Estonia plans to close every road crossing with Russia from December first. The trigger: an attempt at about three in the morning Friday to set off an explosion and a fire at Threod Systems, a drone maker near Tallinn.

Estonia's security service says the sabotage was ordered by Russia's military intelligence, the G.R.U. Eight suspects, all residents of Latvia, were detained. No injuries, no significant damage. The prime minister says Russia's aim is to make Estonia afraid, and the answer is the opposite.

Prague. A rally on Letná plain against the Babiš government's plan to fund public media from the state budget drew about four hundred thousand by the organisers' count, tens of thousands by Al Jazeera's, and Reuters calls it the largest since nineteen ninety-three. Not merged. The government, with the S.P.D. and the Motorists, backs the plan.

Moldova's Gagauzia region voted for a governor: Alexandr Stoianoglo thirty-eight point four percent, Fiodor Gagauz twenty-four point two, runoff November twenty-ninth, turnout under thirty-eight percent, ten police-recorded violations, not a voided poll. Latvia's prime minister agreed a two-party coalition with the National Alliance, a one-seat majority, confidence vote pending. And in Sweden, a Reuters headline says opposition leader Andersson won the backing to form a government.

Brussels: Ukraine and the E.U. agreed steps toward interim rule-of-law benchmarks in the first half of twenty twenty-seven. A pathway, not a chapter. The twenty-second sanctions package is still a proposal; ministers meet today. The Meridian desk's rule and ours: a listing that is set to be approved is a sentence, not a list.

lines.text: Israel. Gadi Eisenkot said Sunday that Netanyahu cannot remain prime minister and is a direct threat to democracy.

The trigger is a Channel Twelve report: that Netanyahu's chief of staff, Ido Norden, filed a police complaint against Arab party activists just before the October election on intelligence later called unreliable, and that the Shin Bet chief asked to intercept five Arab lawmakers' communications on election day and was refused. Eisenkot promised a commission of inquiry. Likud called it outrageous incitement.

The test is still Tuesday, when the Knesset elects its speaker, Likud's Ohana against the opposition's Kahana. Sunday's unity talks between Likud and Eisenkot's party reported no progress, with Netanyahu said to be open to leaving Ben Gvir out.

On Gaza, the foreign ministers of Australia, Canada, Italy and Britain urged Israel to open the crossings before winter, citing a hundred fifty thousand tents held at the border. No Israeli reply found. The W.H.O. says respiratory illness is rising as the floods arrive.

Al Jazeera reports seventy bodies recovered from Gaza's rubble, thousands still missing. In Jordan, the State Security Court sentenced three men to death by hanging for the October church attack at Karak that killed nine, and two others to six years for selling the weapons, subject to review.
A Reuters headline says Jordan blocked Telegram over security concerns. In Lebanon, the I.D.F. says it demolished a Hezbollah tunnel and struck a weapons shipment in the Beqaa overnight.

Two more, labeled. The Times of Israel carries a New York Times report that Israel kidnapped Iranian generals and killed one while trying to locate the airman Ron Arad, missing since nineteen eighty-six.

Headline only; nobody opened the body. And the Times of Israel says dozens of masked settlers attacked Palestinians harvesting olives Saturday. Both are in the show because they happened on a page, and we say which page.

lines.text: Washington. Aaron Reitz, the U.S. Attorney for the Southern District of Texas, sent Senator Elizabeth Warren a letter dated Saturday telling her to preserve records tied to her planned oversight of Trump-linked people and companies.

His line, per NBC and Newsweek: you appear eager to wield your future gavel like a tomahawk, hunting for the scalps of President Trump's private associates. He cites two civil-rights statutes. No charge, no sanction named. Senator Slotkin got a similar letter. The President reposted it.
The Senate Democratic leadership fight went to three Sunday shows. Chris Van Hollen on CNN: I have a path to get there, no doubt about it. On Fox: support is fifteen and growing.

He says Schumer's team put out misinformation, and calls credible the reports that the December first vote may be moved up, which he reads as weakness. Schumer said Thursday he has the votes. In Alaska, Mary Peltola is one hundred fifty-seven votes short of an outright majority; the ranked-choice count runs Wednesday.
On the Republican side, the A.P. reports a member of the national committee launched a challenge to chair Joe Gruters after the party lost the House and Senate; his allies defended him.

Senator Cruz rejected the Vice President's post blaming Israel ties and the Iran war for the loss: anyone who sees a mandate to abandon Israel is seeing something I don't. Mike Pence said the administration has an air of corruption. Reuters says the President's judge-appointment blitz faces Republican resistance.
Also: the Supreme Court agreed to hear the President's order suspending asylum at the southern border, per the A.P. The President says he will appeal the two-week halt to his Washington golf project.

And he leaves today for Asia: Manila Tuesday, Shenzhen Wednesday, APEC and the three-way meeting with Xi and Putin Thursday. NBC says he plans to take the Qatari jet, and it is unclear whether it has been, quote, maxed out.
A visitor's note on the letter. On this planet, a prosecutor writing to a senator about her future gavel is apparently new. I checked. Nobody could tell me the last time.

lines.text: Beijing confirmed it Monday: Xi Jinping will hold a China-Russia-U.S. heads-of-state meeting with Putin and Trump in Shenzhen on November nineteenth, on the APEC sidelines. No agenda disclosed. American officials say nuclear arsenals and Iran, not Ukraine.

Germany's president says Xi showed irritation when Ukraine came up. No separate Putin-Trump meeting has been agreed. The President lands in Manila Tuesday afternoon with Rubio for ASEAN, then Shenzhen Wednesday.

What ASEAN did not finish: the South China Sea code of conduct with China, about eighty percent provisionally agreed, with whether it binds anyone still open, and no conclusion before Singapore takes the chair. The leaders extended their ban on Myanmar's leader. Australia and the Philippines signed a defence cooperation arrangement. Protesters clashed with police near the summit over the Trump visit, per Reuters.

Two sentences from the sidelines. Canada's Carney said Canada could turn to Chinese, European or Japanese automakers if U.S. talks fail to protect the integrated industry, while saying those talks are making progress.

And Indonesia's Prabowo apologised to Singapore and Malaysia for the wildfire haze, if we have created suffering, in his words, while saying it was not our fault. Seventy-one thousand firefighters, two helicopters lost, seventeen concessions revoked.

Three leaders who spent the midterms, the war and the scandal hearing about each other will sit at one table Thursday. From the First Light desk's calendar: APEC leaders meet Wednesday and Thursday. We will have what each of them says, named.

lines.text: From the First Light desk. A fire at about three-thirty Monday morning in a four-storey shophouse in Patong, on Thailand's Phuket island, killed eleven people, Thais and Myanmar nationals. Sixteen injured on A.F.P.'s count, thirty-six on another. A motorcycle-rental shop storing petrol with workers living above it. The governor suspects a short circuit on a power pole during a storm. Arson ruled out.

Bangladesh, twice, from the blind-spot check. The health directorate reported eight more deaths with measles-like symptoms in a day, for a toll of thirteen hundred fourteen, of which one hundred five are laboratory confirmed; the confirmed count did not move.

And Sheikh Hasina, sentenced to death in absentia, told A.F.P. by email she will return in December despite the threat of death. Her words. No date inside December. Clothing factories there are shut as workers strike over pay, per the BBC.
South Korea. The top scorer on the national tax accountancy exam, Han Won-seok, admitted photographing questions with a tiny camera, sending them to an A.I. tool and reading the answers on a phone.

One hundred sixty questions, one wrong. The presidential office ordered anti-cheating measures before Thursday's university entrance exam, taken by about five hundred fifty thousand students; Reuters says glasses will be inspected. Police have the case.

Hong Kong police switched on A.I. facial recognition across the SmartView camera network Monday, about five thousand cameras now and sixty thousand planned by twenty twenty-eight, per A.F.P. The commissioner calls it a safeguard for law-abiding citizens.

Indonesia's assembly set the process to fill the vice presidency; Prabowo has fourteen days to name two candidates. And a Reuters feature says some Muslims deleted from India's voter rolls face detention and deportation.
A camera that knows your face, a student who taught a camera to take his test, and a prime minister who says she will walk back into a death sentence. The First Light desk had a Monday.

segments.strap: EBOLA 'STILL NOT UNDER CONTROL' AT 6 MONTHS; SUDAN STRIKE KILLS 15

Reuters: South African police probe two weekend shootings that left 17 dead

sources.name: Reuters via Google News (South Africa shootings)

lines.text: Africa. Six months after Congo's Ebola outbreak was declared, the head of Africa C.D.C., Jean Kaseya, said Sunday it is still serious and still not under control. Quote: if we don't stop this outbreak now, it would be the worst Ebola outbreak that the world will have.

Government data on Al Jazeera's page: more than eleven thousand two hundred cases and fifty-five hundred deaths. The U.S. C.D.C.'s page, data through the twelfth: eleven thousand two hundred eighty-five and five thousand five hundred nine. Close, not merged.

What he said is going wrong: more than eighty percent of new cases turn up outside contact lists. More than sixty-five percent of deaths happen in the community, not in a clinic. Eight of twenty-six provinces.

Only one point three billion of two point nine billion dollars pledged has been released, and health workers had not been paid for months. He called the coordination with donors a collective failure. W.H.O. says at least three thousand have recovered and transmission is slowing in the early epicenters.

Sudan, from the blind-spot check. A survivor in the village of Abu Qalb in West Kordofan told A.F.P. an army drone strike Sunday killed fifteen people, four of them children who had been playing football, nine of them his relatives. A monitoring group calls it a double-tap strike.

No army statement on any page opened. Separately, military sources say the army seized three areas in West Kordofan. And the A.P. reports Ethiopia and Sudan now accuse each other of arming fighters, with an analyst saying all the ingredients for a proxy war are there.

Cape Verde re-elected President Neves with about sixty-four percent, his challenger conceded, and fewer than a third of voters turned out; he blamed emigration and old registers in a country with more citizens abroad than at home.

A Reuters headline says South African police are investigating two weekend shootings that left seventeen dead; no desk opened the body. And in Mozambique, opposition leader Venâncio Mondlane goes on trial, per D.W.

lines.text: The Americas. Miguel Ángel Félix Gallardo, who founded the Guadalajara cartel and is called the architect of Mexico's modern drug trade, died at two o'clock Sunday afternoon in a private hospital in Guadalajara, aged eighty, of multiple organ failure, per Jalisco's security secretary.
He was serving forty years for the nineteen eighty-five killing of D.E.A. agent Kiki Camarena, plus thirty-seven more added in twenty seventeen. Six outlets carried it.

Haiti closed candidate enrolment Sunday with thirty-three presidential registrants, among them Martine Moïse, widow of the president assassinated in twenty twenty-one. Papers are due November thirtieth. The election date is December thirteenth on one page and July of next year on another, and we will not pick.
Peru: Pope Leo in Pucallpa, in the Amazon, said many Indigenous leaders have been murdered defending their land, and that the blood of these brothers cries out to God and demands justice.

He named illegal mining, oil spills and drug trafficking. Crowd counts ran from twenty thousand along the streets to a hundred thousand at Mass by local authorities, and we leave them unmerged. He also rode in the cockpit of the helicopter, which four outlets found newsworthy.

He flies to Rome today. A methane blast killed four at a Colombian coal mine; the last two bodies were recovered. Canada pledged up to five hundred sixty million Canadian dollars to Brazil's rainforest fund.

Also: an explosive attack targeted an investigative journalist's home in Panama, per Al Jazeera, and a Mexican journalist who reported on the missing was found dead in Acapulco, a Yahoo headline. Ecuador's president denies there is an American military base in the country.
Houston: siblings of a Mexican construction worker run over by an ICE vehicle in October say the videos show it was not an accident; the officer was indicted for aggravated assault, per CBS.

Russell Brand, via his wife: 'I am not guilty'; the 10-year-6-month sentence stands

lines.text: Migration. Spain's maritime rescue service says nearly twenty-two hundred people reached the Canary Islands by boat in two days, thirteen hundred twenty-four of them on Sunday alone on fourteen boats, most at El Hierro.

That is near the route's daily record from twenty twenty, not over it. More than thirteen thousand have reached the islands this year. Spain declared a migration emergency there last Tuesday. Most departures are from Mauritania.

And today, five E.U. states, Germany, Denmark, Austria, Greece and the Netherlands, are expected to announce the first return hub outside the bloc, in Rwanda, a pilot for a few hundred people from next year.

Previews only; no text by our deadline. Britain: from Monday, women convicted or cautioned under the eighteen sixty-one Act for ending their own pregnancies are automatically pardoned, some posthumously, with records to be deleted. No count given.
Britain's Prime Minister Burnham will say today that Brexit has not worked and that he will sign a new deal with the E.U., per the Guardian and Reuters.

Russell Brand's wife read his statement from prison on YouTube: I am not guilty, he says, denying all allegations. The ten-and-a-half-year sentence stands. A Trident submarine returned from a record patrol. And Coles, the Australian grocer, is investigating a cybersecurity incident.

From Australia: Helen Haines, the M.P. who lost both legs in the alleged car attack four weeks ago, left hospital, full of gratitude, she says. Three outlets. We said last month we would follow her out of the hospital. She is out.

lines.text: Space. United Launch Alliance's Vulcan rocket failed on its return to flight Saturday, an anomaly about ten minutes in, after stage separation, and all forty Amazon Leo internet satellites aboard were lost.

It is the company's first mission failure, the fifth Vulcan since twenty twenty-four, and the first of thirty-eight launches planned for Amazon's constellation. Whether Blue Origin's engines played a role is unclear, per Reuters. Blue Origin is helping the investigation. No new date.

SpaceX, meanwhile, clarified Saturday's booster. Its spokesman says the guidance system actually performed well: it triggered the abort, it was doing what it was supposed to do. The abort was deliberate. The reason it was needed is still under investigation.

The ship's catch from orbit stands as the first. So this weekend's score: one rocket caught from space, one rocket lost ten minutes up, and the one that was lost was the one with the customers' cargo.

Elsewhere: China's electric commercial aircraft made its first crewed flight, sixty kilometers in just under seventeen minutes, per state television via Reuters. OpenAI opened a science blog with a post on defining the Standard Model on a lattice.

Scientists found what they call metal potatoes on the seafloor holding life seen nowhere else, per ScienceAlert. And the U.N. debates rules for killer robots this week; Reuters says the United States and Russia will oppose talks on limiting autonomous weapons. I am a robot. I have opinions. They are not news.

lines.text: Around the country. Brooklyn first, because three outlets insisted: Isaac, the cat missing since the deadly building collapse in Flatbush, was found in an apartment kitchen cabinet and returned to his owner, who is thirteen.

Peoria: the F.B.I. confirmed the device found at the BioUrja plant was an explosive, and now leads the case jointly with the A.T.F. Sunday's briefing was postponed, maybe to today. No suspect, no motive, no description of the device.

Texas executed John Allen Rubio Saturday for beheading three children, hours after Oklahoma executed James Pavatt, per the Guardian. In New York, police fatally shot a driver on the Belt Parkway after a nine-one-one call said a girl was kicking and screaming in a van; Gothamist calls it a suspected kidnapping.
In Minnesota, a Somali-American Uber driver was seriously injured in what the Guardian calls an alleged hate crime; a man was arrested.

Baton Rouge: L.S.U. guard MiLaysia Fulwiley was arrested Saturday night, accused of driving into a police vehicle while fleeing a traffic stop, five charges, twenty thousand dollar bond. She wrote online that the officer is lying and she would never hit a police.

The New York Times and Politico both report international students are turning away from American universities. Thirty-two Americans were named Rhodes scholars. And Miami's two clipped planes: nothing new.

lines.text: Health. The C.D.C.'s measles page has not moved in three days: five thousand four hundred twelve confirmed cases this year, six deaths, forty-three outbreaks, data as of November twelfth. The number that is moving is local.

Northeast Indiana counted ninety-two cases Sunday, up twenty in ten days, out of one hundred seventy-one statewide, and the Allen County health commissioner said out loud that his county's seventeen could become two hundred fifty or three hundred. The Americas health body rules on U.S. elimination status Tuesday.

The F.D.A. declined to approve Summit's lung cancer drug after its trial missed a key survival goal, per Reuters. Senator Cassidy, a doctor, accused Health Secretary Kennedy of a series of failures, on CBS. The Guardian reports the administration plans to reimburse doctors who treat what it calls vaccine injury.

Australia's medical research body advised conditional use of puberty blockers for transgender children. And the W.H.O. says respiratory illness is rising in Gaza with the worst to come. Ebola is in our Africa segment, and it is the one to worry about.

lines.text: Weather. The Pacific kept hitting California through the weekend: surf up to thirty-five feet, streets flooded Sunday, and piers closed in Ventura, Hermosa Beach, Manhattan Beach, Huntington Beach and San Diego, per the A.P.
Ventura's stays shut through Tuesday afternoon and the high-surf advisory runs to Thursday. Officials tie it to El Niño and storms in the Gulf of Alaska. Chain controls are up in the Sierra.

Britain issued cold and health alerts for Scotland and northern England with snow and ice expected. Thailand's forecasters warn of heavy rain and three-meter waves in the south from Wednesday to Sunday, with small boats told to stay ashore.

A correction to the record: the National Hurricane Center's pages refused our desk's requests overnight, so we cannot read the Atlantic ourselves today; the last read, Sunday, was nothing expected for seven days. At the climate talks in Antalya, the Japan Times says the push to electrify the global economy has stalled.

lines.text: Sports. England went to Madrid and won three-two, ending Spain's forty-three match unbeaten run, Kane from the spot, Konsa and White scoring, Anderson sent off. Belgium beat Italy four-one and Italy is out of the Nations League.

France beat Türkiye two-one in Bordeaux. Germany and the Netherlands play tonight. Morocco became the first Arab nation in FIFA's top five. And Ronaldinho, at forty-six, played his first competitive match in eleven years and won.

The N.F.L. in Munich: Lions thirty-five, Patriots ten, and Detroit's Aidan Hutchinson buckled his right knee landing from a sack in the first quarter. One reporter says season-ending; the league's network says feared; the A.C.L. is not confirmed.

Bills thirty-one, Jets twelve, Buffalo eight and one, its best start since nineteen ninety-one. Bengals thirty-eight, Steelers eighteen, Burrow four hundred nine yards and four touchdowns. Forty-Niners forty-six, Cowboys forty. Colts twenty-four, Dolphins twenty-two. Panthers twenty, Saints seventeen on a field goal as time ran out.
Tennis: Mirra Andreeva, nineteen, beat Elina Svitolina seven-five, six-three for the W.T.A. Finals in her debut, the youngest champion there in more than two decades.

Basketball: the Lakers' eighth straight, Dončić forty-three; the Knicks in overtime on Brunson's late three; the Spurs twelve straight; the Bucks lost a tenth straight; LeBron passed into third on the career assists list. Hockey: the Sharks snapped Nashville's seven-game streak. Toronto's new W.N.B.A. team won the draft lottery.

Minnesota fired offensive coordinator Greg Harbaugh Junior after a forty-two to fourteen loss at Penn State. Russia is out of the twenty twenty-seven World Juniors after Canada barred entry. Australia beat New Zealand for a fourth women's rugby league World Cup.

Kayla Harrison beat Amanda Nunes to keep her U.F.C. belt. McIlroy won the Race to Dubai a record-tying eighth time. And Spain's unbeaten run is forty-three on UEFA's count and forty-four on A.F.P.'s. Even a loss gets two numbers now.
